title: A public lab notebook, nine pens deep

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Before this blog existed, where did Antoine try out his front-end ideas? On CodePen, where a pen previews instantly and anyone can fork it.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So it's like a public sketchbook for code.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's how he describes it. This page collects nine pens from around 2016 and 2017, the jQuery and plain JavaScript years, each shown as a live embed you can play with.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What kind of things are in there?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Small UI experiments first. A sign-up form, a fake terminal where what you type shows up in the prompt, and a sticky header with jump links. Then widgets: a four-step progress bar, a date range picker with departure and return fields, and a countdown timer that plays a sound at zero.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A countdown that beeps, nice. Anything more ambitious?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: One uses the screen capture feature built into the browser. You start a capture, see a live preview with a red recording border, and a log panel shows the track settings.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I like that it shows what's happening underneath.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Then two bigger demos. The first is a full-screen blackboard on an HTML5 canvas. You pick pen color and size, drag in images, save a P N G, or wipe everything.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A Three dot J S wave. A grid of green cubes moves in a sine wave, and you control the camera with mouse, keyboard, scroll zoom or even a gamepad.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That one's mesmerizing. Why keep them all?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: CodePen taught Antoine to get feedback in under 400 lines. The blackboard and the wave are the ones he reopens when someone asks whether he can prototype a UI fast.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The full page has every embed to try live.
